name: Typical Party in Dorm
description: Today is a holiday in the residence hall — Oleh arrived, in honor of which the girls gave him a string. Oleh liked the gift a lot, so he immediately thought up and offered you, his best friend, the following problem. You are given a string $$$s$$$ of length $$$n$$$, which consists of the first $$$17$$$ lowercase Latin letters {$$$a$$$, $$$b$$$, $$$c$$$, $$$\ldots$$$, $$$p$$$, $$$q$$$} and question marks. And $$$q$$$ queries. Each query is defined by a set of pairwise distinct lowercase first $$$17$$$ letters of the Latin alphabet, which can be used to replace the question marks in the string $$$s$$$. The answer to the query is the sum of the number of distinct substrings that are palindromes over all strings that can be obtained from the original string $$$s$$$ by replacing question marks with available characters. The answer must be calculated modulo $$$998\,244\,353$$$. Pay attention! Two substrings are different when their start and end positions in the string are different. So, the number of different substrings that are palindromes for the string aba will be $$$4$$$: a , b , a , aba . Consider examples of replacing question marks with letters. For example, from the string aba??ee when querying {$$$a$$$, $$$b$$$} you can get the strings ababaee or abaaaee but you cannot get the strings pizza , abaee , abacaba , aba?fee , aba47ee , or abatree . Recall that a palindrome is a string that reads the same from left to right as from right to left.
input_specification: The first line contains a single integer $$$n$$$ ($$$1 \le n \le 1\,000$$$) — the length of the string $$$s$$$. The second line contains the string $$$s$$$, which consists of $$$n$$$ lowercase Latin letters and question marks. It is guaranteed that all letters in the string belong to the set {$$$a$$$, $$$b$$$, $$$c$$$, $$$\ldots$$$, $$$p$$$, $$$q$$$}. The third line contains a single integer $$$q$$$ ($$$1 \le q \le 2 \cdot 10^5$$$) — the number of queries. This is followed by $$$q$$$ lines, each containing a single line $$$t$$$ — a set of characters that can replace question marks ($$$1 \le |t| \le 17$$$). It is guaranteed that all letters in the string belong to the set {$$$a$$$, $$$b$$$, $$$c$$$, $$$\ldots$$$, $$$p$$$, $$$q$$$} and occur at most once.
output_specification: For each query print one number — the total numbers of palindromic substrings in all strings that can be obtained from the string $$$s$$$, modulo $$$998\,244\,353$$$.

approach_summary: Define state dp[mask][i] capturing the subset of visited/chosen elements. Transition by iterating over valid unset bits in O(2^N × N) time.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 1679E — Typical Party in Dorm [450. Bitmask DP]
topic_editorial.summary: Bitmask DP state compression over subsets.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: Because the dimension $N$ is small ($N \le 20$), each subset of chosen or visited elements can be encoded compactly into a single bitmask integer $0 \le \text{mask} < 2^N$. The optimal substructure property guarantees that to extend a subset $\text{mask}$, we only need to know the current subset and optionally the last added element.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: State Definition
Define $dp[\text{mask}]$ (or $dp[\text{mask}][u]$ if the last visited element matters) as:
- $dp[\text{mask}] = $ the optimal value obtainable using the subset of elements represented by the bitmask $\text{mask}$.

### Step 2: Base Cases
- Initialize all DP states to a sentinel value (e.g. $\infty$ for minimization, or $-\infty$ for maximization).
- Base state: $dp[0] = 0$ (empty configuration has cost zero).

### Step 3: Recurrence Relation & Transitions
For every mask from $0$ to $2^N - 1$:
If the state $dp[\text{mask}]$ is reachable:
For every element $i \in [0, N-1]$ such that the $i$-th bit is NOT set in $\text{mask}$ ($(\text{mask} \mathbin{\&} (1 \ll i)) == 0$):
$$\text{next\_mask} = \text{mask} \mid (1 \ll i)$$
$$dp[\text{next\_mask}] = \text{opt}\big(dp[\text{next\_mask}], dp[\text{mask}] + \text{cost}(\text{mask}, i)\big)$$

### Step 4: Final Answer
The final answer is stored in $dp[(1 \ll N) - 1]$, which corresponds to all $N$ elements being chosen.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(2^N \cdot N)$
  There are $2^N$ total bitmasks. From each mask, we iterate over at most $N$ possible next bits to transition. For $N = 20$, $2^{20} \cdot 20 \approx 2 \times 10^7$ operations, which easily runs in $\approx 0.15$ seconds.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(2^N)$
  Storing the DP table for all $2^N$ configurations requires $2^{20} \times 8$ bytes $\approx 8\text{ MB}$ of memory, well below 256 MB.
